# Philip Rubin
Philip Rubin is a distinguished researcher in experimental psychology and linguistics, best known for his foundational work on speech synthesis and perception. Starting in the early 1970s, he developed computational models at Haskins Laboratories, including the ASY articulatory synthesis program, which introduced the concept of "speech gestures" to describe and control articulatory events. He also designed the SWS sinewave synthesis system, the first to create stimuli for large-scale perceptual experiments by replacing formants with pure tones, and contributed to the development of the HADES signal processing system and the SPIEL programming language. His theoretical contributions emphasize a dynamical systems perspective on speech, focusing on spatiotemporal coordination and embodied constraints rather than traditional signal features.
Beyond his research, Rubin has held significant leadership roles in science policy and administration. He served as the Director of the NSF's Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences (2000–2003) and later as a senior advisor in the Directorate for Social, Behavioral and Economic Sciences. In February 2012, he became the Assistant Director for Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), where he led the White House's neuroscience initiative and co-chaired the National Science and Technology Council's Committee on Science. He retired from OSTP in 2015 and has since remained active in science advocacy, serving on various advisory boards and committees related to human subjects research, ethics, and STEM education.
